description: We're a family team from Riyadh: me and my 11-year-old cousin. We love space and games, and we're excited to build something that teaches kids how real missions work. We bring creativity, research and storytelling, plus a young teammate who knows exactly what kids find fun.
summary:
Red Planet Outpost is a free browser game, in English and Arabic, where kids aged 7 to 12 command a Mars outpost for 30 sols. Each sol, the solar panels make just 9 units of power, and players split them between life support, the greenhouse, a radiation shield, the radio to Earth and science. No choice is free: every unit spent on safety is a unit lost for science.
It answers the challenge by grounding every risk in real NASA data. Solar storms come from NASA DONKI, including live forecasts of eruptions heading to Mars, and radiation follows Curiosity RAD measurements, like the 8,100 µGy storm of 20 May 2024. Players also face steady cosmic rays and can cover the habitat in Mars soil, trading power now for safety later. Dr. Rana, a talking scientist, explains the real event behind each sol.
This matters because 86% of children are interested in space, yet most content for them is too abstract, too technical, or fun but inaccurate. Our game lets kids practise the decisions behind a real mission, not just see its outcome.
details:
Red Planet Outpost turns real NASA space-weather and radiation data into a survival game for kids aged 7 to 12. Players don't just learn facts about Mars: they make the same trade-offs NASA mission planners make, and they see the results of every choice.

 

1. WHAT IT DOES

The player picks a commander and runs a Mars outpost in Gale Crater for 30 sols (a sol is one Mars day). Every sol follows three steps:

1) Read Earth's space-weather forecast.

2) Split 9 units of solar power between five systems: life support, the greenhouse, the radiation shield, the radio to Earth, and science.

3) See what happens to the crew's air, food, radiation dose and science.

 

The crew wins by keeping air and food above zero and the radiation dose under a safety budget for all 30 sols. Stars reward the science sent home to Earth. Each system covers an area the challenge asks for:

- Life support: the air drops if it gets less than 3 power a sol.

- Food production: the greenhouse needs 2 power a sol, plus a "harvest the lettuce now or wait" decision.

- Power budgeting: 9 solar units a sol (5 in dust storms, 3 with the panels folded away), plus a small battery for leftover power.

- Radiation shielding: the shield blocks up to 85% of the particles from solar storms, but only up to 20% of cosmic rays. Covering the habitat with Mars soil cuts cosmic rays by 30%, at a cost of 2 power a sol for 3 sols.

- Communication delay: the radio must be on to receive tomorrow's forecast and send science home, and the game shows the real Earth-Mars message delay. One decision asks: wait a sol for Mission Control's answer, or fix the problem yourself and risk making it worse?

 

Decision cards turn real mission dilemmas into choices. When a dust storm rolls in, the player has 15 seconds to fold the solar panels (lose power now) or leave them out (risk them being buried). Others include a spacewalk to clean dusty panels (more power, but extra radiation) and a crew workout against bone loss (healthier crew, but extra power).

 

2. HOW IT WORKS

The game has two modes:

- Storm Season replays the real solar storms of May 2024, day by day, building up to the 20 May storm that NASA's Curiosity rover measured at 8,100 µGy.

- Live Sun downloads the last 30 days of NASA space weather when the game loads, so the real Sun sets the mission's risk.

 

From NASA's data, the game keeps only the events strong enough to matter: X-class and strong M-class flares, fast solar eruptions, eruptions predicted to hit Mars, and major geomagnetic storms. Each day becomes one sol with a danger level from 0 to 3. The forecast gives a chance, not a promise, just like real space weather. Radiation follows Curiosity's real measurements: about 210 µGy a day from cosmic rays, and 8,100 µGy on the storm day.

 

After every sol, a scientist character, Dr. Rana, names the real NASA event and explains it in kid-friendly language, read aloud in English or Arabic. At the end, a debrief explains what the player learned, including where the game simplifies real numbers to stay playable.

 

3. HOW WE TESTED IT

A Python bot played 1,000 missions (200 for each of 5 strategies) to check that the game rewards good thinking and that no choice is free. Never shielding survived 0% of missions; a low shield every sol, 7%; a medium shield every sol, 68%; reading NASA's forecast and shielding up on storm days, 78%; reading the forecast and covering the habitat with Mars soil, 94%. Reading the forecast also sent home about a third more science than shielding on medium every sol. That is exactly the lesson: using real data lets you stay safe without wasting power. Our co-designer, Renda (age 11, in our target age group), play-tested the game.

 

4. BENEFITS

- Kids practise how scientists think: reading data, weighing trade-offs, planning ahead and living with the consequences.

- They learn real science, such as why Mars is dangerous without a magnetic field and why astronauts would bury their homes in soil, from real NASA measurements.

- It's free, with no download or account, and runs in any web browser on a computer, tablet or phone.

- It works in Arabic and English, so many more children can use it in their own language.

- The code is open source (MIT licence), so schools and teachers can host, adapt or translate it.

 

5. INTENDED IMPACT

Kids already love space: 86% of children aged 8 to 12 are interested in space exploration (Harris Poll for the LEGO Group, 2019). Our goal is to turn that passion into a scientist's mindset, by letting kids practise the decisions behind a mission, not just see its outcome. In Saudi Arabia, it supports the young space talent that Vision 2030 calls for, and teaches the same space weather that the Saudi satellite Shams studies. Next, we plan to add recorded Arabic narration, real NASA life-support figures, a Moon mode, ISS radiation data from NASA RadLab, and classroom testing to measure what kids learn.

 

6. HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- A living simulation, not a quiz: every choice costs something, and the effects build up over 30 sols.

- The real Sun sets the danger: in Live Sun mode, NASA's latest space weather decides how risky your mission is, so no two weeks play the same.

- Two kinds of radiation: bursts of solar particles can be blocked with a shield on the day, while steady cosmic rays need a long-term plan, like covering the habitat in Mars soil.

- Urgency: timed decisions, like the 15-second dust-storm choice, make the trade-offs feel real.

- "This really happened": every event ends with Dr. Rana naming the real NASA event behind it, linking play to real science.

 

7. FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age 7 to 12: plain words, big buttons, only five systems to manage, and explanations read aloud for younger readers.

- No free choice: we tested the game with 1,000 missions so that no strategy is safe without a cost.

- Honest science: real data is labelled "Real event" or "Live", and the game explains where it simplifies numbers.

- Access: free, no download, no account, and in Arabic and English with a right-to-left layout for Arabic. Storm Season mode needs no live data.

- Inclusion: every child can be the commander, girl or boy.

- Learning from failure: each mission is different, so kids can try new strategies without feeling punished.

- Privacy and safety: there are no accounts and no server, so no personal data leaves the player's device, and no images or voices of children are used.

 

8. TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, in a single web page with no server.

- NASA data access: NASA Open APIs (api.nasa.gov).

- Browser features: Web Audio for sound, and Web Speech for Dr. Rana's voice.

- Hosting: GitHub Pages, with the code on GitHub.

- Testing: Python with Playwright, for the 1,000-mission test bot.

- AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic), as a coding and writing assistant (see "Use of AI").

- Hardware: none special. We built it on laptops, and it runs on any device with a web browser.
